newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia must do more to scrap last sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia must do more to scrap last sanctions.

text.p: Yugoslavia, shattered by a four-year trade embargo, is struggling to dismantle an "outer wall" of sanctions and gain access to urgently needed capital to revive its stagnant economy.

But diplomats warned that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialist government was not doing enough to meet the international community's conditions for the country to be fully rehabiliated.
"The government knows exactly what it has to do for the outer wall of sanctions to be removed. Nobody will do it for them," one Western diplomat, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
"There has been some positive change in the political atmosphere but that is not enough," he added.
The U.S. kept an outer wall of sanctions on Belgrade after a U.N. trade embargo imposed on Serbia in 1992 for its role in the Bosnian war lifted last October.
The remaining restrictions prevent Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, from rejoining international organisations and financial institutions and gaining access to foreign funds.

Their removal has been made dependent on Belgrade's respect of human rights in its mostly-Albanian southern province of Kosovo, its cooperation with The Hague war crimes tribunal, progress in talks with other former Yugoslav republics on division of assets of the old federation and moves to widen democracy in the country.
So far the only positive move by Milosevic was his recognition of the opposition's victory in local elections last November, after three months of mass demonstrations at home and pressure abroad.

Diplomats criticised Milosevic's Socialists for not attending U.S-brokered talks between the Kosovo Albanian leadership and Serbs in early April in New York, marking the beginning of the required political dialogue.
The entire Serbian opposition was present but Milosevic's Socialists dropped out at the last minute, insisting the Kosovo issue was an internal matter and should be discussed at home.

"If the Socialists had been present, as they should have been, the Yugoslav government would have received some credit for that development and it would have helped in the step-by-step process needed to satisfy the requirements for lifting the outer ring of sanctions," one diplomat said.
Diplomats expressed hope the Socialists would participate at the next meeting expected to be held in a few months.

Belgrade has failed to cooperate with The Hague war crimes tribunal, and its insistance of being the sole successor state to the old Yugoslav federation and blocking the succession issue have also helped cement the outer wall of sanctions.

One diplomat expressed the fear that with elections due by the end of the year, and prompting Milosevic to play the nationalist card, there was little likelihood of early progress on the issues that could free the country from its last santions.
